title: DTCC project in focus: Reclaimed, Redesigned, Re-twinned
abstract: Large amounts of building materials are discarded every year, not because they lack value, but because they don’t meet the standards. Through digital twins, advanced scanning and new design workflows, the DTCC project Reclaimed, Redesigned, Re-Twinned explores how these materials can become a natural part of future construction.

body:
In the construction industry, large volumes of materials are discarded yearly simply because they do not meet standard formats. The DTCC research project Reclaimed, Redesigned, Re-Twinned, led by Malgorzata Zboinska, aims to change that by developing digital workflows that make it possible to reuse irregular and damaged components like broken bricks, windows or random pieces of wood in new buildings. By integrating digital twin technology into architectural workflows, materials can be scanned, analyzed, and reassembled digitally before being used in physical construction.

“We want to enable architects and other actors to work more effectively with reclaimed materials that are not standardized. Today, a large share of these materials is downcycled or sent to landfills, even though they still hold significant value. We need to change this, both for environmental and economic reasons”, says Malgorzata Zboinska, research lead of the DTCC project Reclaimed, redesigned, Re-Twinned.

By embedding information such as geometry, condition, cost, and environmental impact into digital models, architects can evaluate different design options early in the process. This provides a clearer basis for comparing alternatives and supports more informed decisions.
“With digital twins, we can simulate different ways of assembling materials and understand not only how a design will look, but also how much it will cost and what environmental impact it will have. That creates a much stronger basis for decision-making”, says Malgorzata Zboinska.

**Taking the research to the next level**

In the first phase of DTCC, Malgorzata was research lead for the project Twin Re-Fab, focusing on testing early workflows and tools. The researchers worked with individual components and explored digital twin scanning. While Reclaimed, Redesigned, Re-Twinned is a natural continuation of the project, the research is performed at a larger scale.

“In the previous project, we created the foundation by testing workflows for scanning and redesigning individual components. Now we are scaling that up and looking at entire building component systems, such as walls, slabs and pillars, investigating more types of reclaimed materials and larger quantities. It is a big and important step forward”, says Malgorzata Zboinska.

**From scanning to design and fabrication**

A key part of the project is capturing detailed data from reclaimed materials. Using robotic scanning technologies, the research team can create high-resolution digital representations of irregular components, which can then be integrated into computational design tools and digital manufacturing pipelines.

“These materials are often complex, so we need more advanced methods for capturing their geometry and properties. It can be broken material, bits of something that used to be a wall for example. Robotic scanning allows us to do that in a safe and flexible way”, says Malgorzata Zboinska.

Once digitized, the materials can be used in parametric design tools that generate and evaluate multiple design alternatives. The project also explores robotic machining and 3D printing of custom connectors, enabling new ways of assembling materials that would otherwise be difficult to reuse.

“We are not only looking at how to design with these materials, but also how to physically realize the solutions. For example, we can introduce custom joining elements that make it possible to connect irregular pieces in a structurally sound and waste-free way. With this appraoch, we can create whole new building components out of something broken”, she says.

**Testing in a real-world case**

The research is carried out in close collaboration with industry partners, including Liljewall Architects and Stena Fastigheter, and is applied to a real re-development project in Gothenburg. Materials from an existing industrial site will be analyzed and reused as part of the transformation into a residential area.

“This gives us a unique opportunity to test our methods on a real case. The real-life research setting allows us to experiment and iterate in ways that would not be possible in a standard construction project. I hope it will bring us the important insights needed to, in time, broadly integrate the tools into the everyday workflows of architects and decision makers”, says Malgorzata Zboinska.
